segments.say: Earlier tonight, back on that platform with Jonah, we asked a curious question. Can believing something about stress change what it does to you? Now we can finally look at the answer. And it starts with a very large survey of ordinary people in the United States.

In 2012, Abiola Keller and her colleagues at the University of Wisconsin looked at data from almost twenty nine thousand adults. Years earlier, as part of a national health survey, these people had answered two simple questions. How much stress had they experienced in the past year? And how much did they think stress affected their health?

show.what: Nearly 29,000 adults: stress, beliefs about stress, and later health records

segments.say: The researchers then linked those answers to national records of who had died in the years that followed. It's a sombre measure, but a very solid one. And what they found surprised a lot of people.

People who reported a lot of stress, and who also believed that stress was affecting their health a lot, had a forty three percent higher risk of dying early, compared with people who reported little stress.

show.title: High stress plus the belief that it was harming them
show.label: higher risk of dying early

segments.say: But here's the part that caught everyone's attention. People who reported just as much stress, but who did not believe it was harming their health much, did not show that higher risk. In fact, they had some of the lowest risk in the whole study.

In other words, in this data, stress on its own wasn't the strongest warning sign. Stress combined with the belief that it was doing harm was. The researchers estimated that over the years of the study, many deaths in the United States were linked with that combination, not with stress by itself.

Now, we need to be careful. This was a survey, not an experiment. Perhaps people who felt stress was damaging them were already unwell, and could feel it. Perhaps they had harder kinds of stress. A finding like this can't prove that a belief, on its own, changes health. It raises a question. So researchers went looking for experiments.
One of the best known came from Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor, published in 2013.

They worked with employees of a large company during a stressful period. Some watched a few short videos explaining that stress can be enhancing, that it can sharpen focus, deepen connections and help people grow. Others watched videos explaining that stress is debilitating and harmful. A third group watched no videos at all.

show.who: Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor
show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2013
show.what: Short videos framing stress as helpful or as harmful

segments.say: Over the next weeks, the people who had seen the stress-is-enhancing videos reported fewer psychological symptoms, like anxiety and low mood, and said their work was going better, than the people in the other groups. Nothing about their workload had changed. Only the story they had heard about what stress is for.

Picture a quiet windowsill on a busy morning. The day ahead is just as full as it was. But the way you hold it in your mind, as a threat, or as a challenge you're getting ready for, can change how it feels to walk into it.

show.cap: A different story about the same feeling

segments.say: Another line of research looked at the physical feeling of stress itself. The pounding heart, the butterflies, the dry mouth. What if those sensations aren't a sign that something is going wrong?

In 2010, Jeremy Jamieson and his colleagues worked with students preparing for the GRE, a big entrance exam for graduate school in the United States. Before a practice test, half the students were told something simple. People think feeling anxious during a test makes them do worse, but research suggests that arousal doesn't hurt, and can even help. If you feel anxious, that could be helping you.

show.what: Students told that a racing heart can help them did better on practice maths questions

segments.say: The students who heard that message did better on the maths questions than the students who hadn't. And when the researchers later asked about the real exam, taken weeks afterwards, the same group reported better maths scores there too. The researchers gave their paper a lovely title. Turning the knots in your stomach into bows.

It's a gentle image, and a useful one. The knots are still there. The same physical feeling, the same racing heart. But tied in a different way, they can hold something together instead of pulling it tight.

show.text: Turning the knots in your stomach into bows
show.by: Title of Jamieson and colleagues' 2010 paper

segments.say: In later work, published in 2012, Jamieson and his colleagues found that rethinking stress like this changed the body's response as well. People who saw their racing heart as fuel tended to show a more efficient pattern, with the heart pumping strongly and the blood vessels staying more relaxed, rather than the tighter pattern linked to feeling threatened.
And then there's a very small sentence, studied by Alison Wood Brooks, published in 2014.

Brooks asked people to do things that make most of us nervous. Sing in front of others. Give a short speech on camera. Solve hard maths problems under time pressure. Just before starting, some people were asked to say out loud, I am anxious. Others said, I am calm. And others said, I am excited.

show.what: Saying "I am excited" before a nerve-racking task

segments.say: In her studies, the people who said I am excited tended to do better, and felt more excited, than the people who tried to tell themselves to calm down. Brooks's idea was that anxiety and excitement feel very similar in the body. Both are high energy. So it may be an easier step to move from anxious to excited, than to try to jump all the way down to calm.

So, the idea in short. Stress can be read as a signal that something matters, and not only as a warning that something's wrong. A racing heart can be fuel for the task. And when you're nervous, excited may be a closer and kinder place to aim for than calm.

show.title: The stress mindset, in short
items: Stress can be a signal, not only a warning
A racing heart can be fuel
Excited is closer to anxious than calm is

segments.say: Now, here's the honest part. These findings are encouraging, and they've become very popular. But in science, popular and settled are not the same thing.

When other researchers have tried similar mindset interventions in larger groups, the effects have often been smaller than in the first studies, and some attempts haven't found much at all. A belief can't make a dangerous situation safe, or turn years of hardship into something easy. And no one should feel that their stress is their own fault for thinking about it the wrong way.

What seems to survive is something more modest. How we interpret the feeling of stress can shift, a little, how we respond to it. Not a magic trick. More like adjusting the angle of a sail, when you can't change the wind.

So let's be clear about what a belief can't do. It can't make a dangerous situation safe. It can't remove real hardship, like illness, loss or loneliness. And it never makes anyone to blame for the stress they feel. A kinder story about stress is a small tool, not a test you can fail.

show.title: What a belief can't do
items: Make anyone to blame for their stress

segments.say: And so, at five to nine, Jonah arrives, a little breathless, outside the meeting room. His heart is pounding. His mouth is dry. And for a moment, the old thought appears. This is bad. I'm going to fall apart.

Then he remembers something he once read. He takes a breath and says to himself, quietly. This is my body getting ready. I'm excited. The pounding doesn't stop. But it feels different now. Less like a warning, more like an engine warming up.

And as he opens the door, he sees a familiar face near the front, someone who smiles and gives him a small nod. Because there's one more thing that changes how stress lands on us, perhaps the oldest of all. And that's the people around us.
